blocks.text: …I followed the property manager, a soft-spoken man named Mr. Doyle, into the pool house while thirty children shrieked on a bouncy castle outside.

In 1998, my late husband, Frank, had quietly bought a twelve-acre parcel outside Franklin as an investment and placed it in a trust in my name, using my maiden name, Collins. He told me only that he'd "put a little something away for us." Frank died in 2011. I assumed the investment had been small.

In 2016, the trust leased one acre of that land, the acre under this house, to a developer on a long-term ground lease. The developer was my son-in-law, Christopher. The trust's paperwork listed Christopher as trustee, with a signature that was supposed to be mine authorizing it. It wasn't.

For eight years, Christopher had been collecting rent from the other eleven acres, which he'd subleased to a landscaping company and a storage business, and paying himself, the trustee, a management fee that ate almost all of it.
He'd paid only a token amount for the ground under his own house.

Mr. Doyle sighed. The trust Frank set up had a clause: it couldn't be dissolved while a minor grandchild was named as a beneficiary. Frank had added it to protect Sophie's future. Christopher had found the clause and amended the trust documents to name Sophie as the primary beneficiary, with himself as her guardian and trustee, which made it nearly impossible for anyone to close the trust or take it away from him until she turned twenty-one.
Mr. Doyle had worked for Frank thirty years earlier and recognized my maiden name the moment the event planner read it out. He'd always suspected something was wrong with the paperwork.
I didn't make a scene. I went out to the backyard and watched Sophie blow out ten candles.
Then I took my daughter, Amanda, aside and showed her the documents. She hadn't known. She thought the house had been paid for with Christopher's bonus.

With a lawyer's help, the forged trustee appointment was voided. A court restored me as trustee and ordered Christopher to repay most of what he'd taken. Amanda filed for separation. The twenty-five-hundred-dollar "contribution" he'd charged me, and several other guests, went back to everyone.

I kept Sophie as a beneficiary, the way Frank intended. When she turns twenty-one, the land will help pay for whatever she wants to become. She says she wants to be a lawyer. I told her she already has her first case.
